{{Short description|Associative algebra with lifting property}}

In abstract algebra, a '''quasi-free algebra''' is an [[associative algebra]] that satisfies the lifting property similar to that of a [[formally smooth algebra]] in [[commutative algebra]]. The notion was introduced by [[Joachim Cuntz|Cuntz]] and [[Daniel Quillen|Quillen]] for the applications to [[cyclic homology]].<ref>{{harvnb|Cuntz|Quillen|1995}}</ref> A quasi-free algebra generalizes a [[free algebra]], as well as the [[coordinate ring]] of a smooth affine [[complex curve]]. Because of the latter generalization, a quasi-free algebra can be thought of as signifying smoothness on a [[noncommutative space]].<ref>{{harvnb|Cuntz|2013|loc=Introduction}}</ref>

== Definition ==
Let ''A'' be an associative algebra over the complex numbers. Then ''A'' is said to be ''quasi-free'' if the following equivalent conditions are met:<ref name="definition">{{harvnb|Cuntz|Quillen|1995|loc=Proposition 3.3.}}</ref><ref>{{harvnb|Vale|2009|loc=Proposotion 7.7.}}</ref><ref>{{harvnb|Kontsevich|Rosenberg|2000|loc=1.1.}}</ref>
*Given a [[square-zero extension]] <math>R \to R/I</math>, each homomorphism <math>A \to R/I</math> lifts to <math>A \to R</math>.
*The cohomological dimension of ''A'' with respect to [[Hochschild cohomology]] is at most one.

Let <math>(\Omega A, d)</math> denotes the [[differential envelope]] of ''A''; i.e., the universal [[Differential graded algebra|differential-graded algebra]] generated by ''A''.<ref>{{harvnb|Cuntz|Quillen|1995|loc=Proposition 1.1.}}</ref><ref>{{harvnb|Kontsevich|Rosenberg|2000|loc=1.1.2.}}</ref> Then ''A'' is quasi-free if and only if <math>\Omega^1 A</math> is [[projective module|projective]] as a [[bimodule]] over ''A''.<ref name="definition" />

There is also a characterization in terms of a connection. Given an ''A''-bimodule ''E'', a [[right connection]] on ''E'' is a linear map
:<math>\nabla_r : E \to E \otimes_A \Omega^1 A</math>
that satisfies <math>\nabla_r(as) = a \nabla_r(s)</math> and <math>\nabla_r(sa) = \nabla_r(s) a + s \otimes da</math>.<ref>{{harvnb|Vale|2009|loc=Definition 8.4.}}</ref> A left connection is defined in the similar way. Then ''A'' is quasi-free if and only if <math>\Omega^1 A</math> admits a right connection.<ref>{{harvnb|Vale|2009|loc=Remark 7.12.}}</ref>

== Properties and examples ==
One of basic properties of a quasi-free algebra is that the algebra is left and right [[hereditary ring|hereditary]] (i.e., a [[submodule]] of a projective left or right module is projective or equivalently the left or right global dimension is at most one).<ref>{{harvnb|Cuntz|Quillen|1995|loc=Proposition 5.1.}}</ref> This puts a strong restriction for algebras to be quasi-free. For example, a hereditary (commutative) [[integral domain]] is precisely a [[Dedekind domain]]. In particular, a [[polynomial ring]] over a field is quasi-free if and only if the number of variables is at most one.

An analog of the [[tubular neighborhood theorem]], called the ''formal tubular neighborhood theorem'', holds for quasi-free algebras.<ref>{{harvnb|Cuntz|Quillen|1995|loc=§ 6.}}</ref>
